211.event_title: Jonas Salk's polio vaccine is released without a patent
211.event: On 12 April 1955 the polio vaccine developed by Jonas Salk's team at the University of Pittsburgh, with funding from the public donations of the March of Dimes, was announced as safe and effective. Asked in a television interview with Edward R. Murrow who owned the patent, Salk answered that there was no patent and that the vaccine belonged to the people. He declined to patent it or profit from it, and the vaccine was soon used around the world.
211.explanation: One of the twentieth century's most important medical advances was given to the public rather than treated as private property.
211.tie_back: The kural says that true duty to others expects nothing in return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain-cloud, and Salk's vaccine reached the world with no return sought for him.
211._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of benefit given without seeking return, tempered by historians' observation that a patent may not have been obtainable in any case.

212.event_title: Alfred Nobel leaves his fortune to fund the Nobel Prizes
212.event: Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist and industrialist who had built a fortune from dynamite and other inventions, signed his last will at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris on 27 November 1895. It directed that most of his estate be invested and the income awarded each year as prizes to those who had conferred the greatest benefit on humankind in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace. After Nobel's death in 1896 the will met opposition from relatives and others, and the first prizes were awarded in 1901.
212.explanation: A fortune built over a lifetime of industrial work was turned, by one document, into a permanent reward for those who benefit the world.
212.tie_back: The kural says that wealth earned by hard and persistent effort exists to help the deserving, and Nobel's will directed his earnings to the people who most benefit humanity.
212._accuracy_note: A close fit to wealth earned by effort and given to the worthy, though the gift came only after Nobel's death.

213.event_title: Edward Jenner's free vaccinations in the Temple of Vaccinia
213.event: After his first vaccination experiment against smallpox on 14 May 1796, the country doctor Edward Jenner used a small rustic hut in the garden of his home at Berkeley, which he named the Temple of Vaccinia, to vaccinate the poor of the district free of charge. He did not patent his discovery, and he shared cowpox material and his findings widely with other doctors. The Wellcome Collection describes the hut as the world's first free vaccination clinic, and vaccination eventually led to the global eradication of smallpox, declared in 1980.
213.explanation: Jenner's discovery and his free clinic began a chain of benefit that reached every part of the world.
213.tie_back: The kural says no good on earth or in heaven equals helping others as the world rightly expects, and few acts of help have spread as widely as vaccination freely given.
213._accuracy_note: Jenner's work shows beneficence of unequalled reach, but the kural's claim is a comparative ranking of virtues that no single event can prove.

214.event_title: Ida Scudder builds a hospital and medical school for women at Vellore
214.event: Ida Scudder, born in India to an American missionary family, qualified in medicine at Cornell in 1899 and returned to Vellore, where after her father's death she began treating women in a small room of the mission bungalow. With money she had raised in America she opened a small hospital in 1902, started training nurses by 1909, ran roadside clinics for villages, and in 1918 opened the Union Mission Medical School for Women. The school became the Christian Medical College, Vellore, which was affiliated to the University of Madras by 1950 and grew into one of India's leading medical institutions.
214.explanation: Scudder spent five decades building institutions shaped around the needs of the society she lived in, especially women who could not be treated by male doctors.
214.tie_back: The kural says that only the person who understands what is fitting towards the world, and acts on it, is truly alive, and Scudder's life was spent doing exactly what her community most needed.
214._accuracy_note: Her life is a fine example of living for the world's good, but the kural's sharp contrast with those who are 'counted among the dead' has no direct counterpart in the event.

215.event: The Rani-ki-Vav, or Queen's Stepwell, on the banks of the Saraswati River at Patan, was built in the 11th century and is traditionally attributed to Queen Udayamati as a memorial to the Chaulukya king Bhima I. UNESCO describes it as a memorial that also functions as a single water management system, designed as an inverted temple with seven levels of stairs leading down to an underground reservoir and decorated with hundreds of sculptures. Silted over for centuries, it was excavated and restored by the Archaeological Survey of India and inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2014.
215.explanation: Royal wealth was turned into a monumental public reservoir, combining remembrance of a king with a store of water for the community.
215.tie_back: The kural compares the wealth of a wise person who loves the world to the village tank filled to the brim, and the stepwell is literally royal wealth turned into a great public store of water.
215._accuracy_note: The image of the full village tank fits remarkably well, though the queen's personal motives and the stepwell's exact use are not documented in detail.

216.event_title: George Peabody founds the Peabody Donation Fund for London's poor
216.event: George Peabody, an American-born banker who had made his fortune in London, wrote to The Times in March 1862 announcing a gift of 150,000 pounds, later increased, to improve the condition of the poor of London. The trustees of the Peabody Donation Fund used it to build model dwellings for working people, with running water and decent sanitation at affordable rents, and the first block opened in Spitalfields in 1864. The trust he founded still exists today as one of London's oldest and largest housing associations.
216.explanation: A private fortune was set up as a lasting public resource in the heart of the city, where the people who needed it could reach it.
216.tie_back: The kural compares the wealth of a generous person to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the village, where everyone can pick its fruit, and Peabody placed his wealth in the midst of London's working poor.
216._accuracy_note: The accessibility and lasting yield of the gift fit the fruit-tree image well, although the housing was rented and selective rather than open to everyone.

217.event_title: Nicolas Rolin and Guigone de Salins found the Hotel-Dieu of Beaune
217.event: In 1443 Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy, and his wife Guigone de Salins founded the Hotel-Dieu at Beaune as a hospital for the poor, at a time when much of the town's population was destitute and the area had recently suffered an outbreak of plague. The building was dedicated on 31 December 1451 and received its first patients the next day, cared for by a community of nursing sisters, and Guigone de Salins continued to direct it after her husband's death until her own death in 1470. The hospital went on caring for patients for more than five centuries before becoming a museum.
217.explanation: The fortune of one of the most powerful men in Burgundy was turned into a hospital that served the sick poor for over five hundred years.
217.tie_back: The kural compares the wealth of a noble person to a medicinal tree that never fails to heal, and the Hotel-Dieu turned the Rolins' wealth into healing for generation after generation.
217._accuracy_note: A close and durable match to wealth that heals others, though the founders' private motives, sometimes debated, are not part of the documented record used here.

218.event_title: Pestalozzi keeps serving poor children after his Neuhof school fails
218.event: In the 1770s the Swiss educator Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi and his wife Anna took poor children into their farm, the Neuhof, teaching them spinning, weaving and farming alongside their lessons, but the farm could not support them and the venture never brought him much money. Pestalozzi did not abandon the work: after French troops invaded Switzerland, he gathered more than eighty orphaned and destitute children at Stans in 1799, caring for them himself in a deserted convent until the French reclaimed the building in June 1799. He went on to become one of the founders of modern education.
218.explanation: Financial failure did not end Pestalozzi's commitment to poor children; it continued in even harder conditions.
218.tie_back: The kural says those who understand their duty do not slacken in helping others even when their means have shrunk, and Pestalozzi returned to caring for destitute children after his own resources had failed.
218._accuracy_note: A good fit to helping on with diminished means, though the sources describe his means as never ample rather than a dramatic fall from wealth.

219.event_title: Oseola McCarty gives her life savings for scholarships
219.event: Oseola McCarty, who left school in the sixth grade and spent most of her life washing and ironing other people's clothes by hand, gave 150,000 dollars, most of her life savings, to the University of Southern Mississippi in 1995 to fund scholarships for students in financial need. Asked about the gift, she said she did not regret any of it and only wished she had more to give. Local businesses and donors around the world added to the fund, and she received the Presidential Citizens Medal from President Bill Clinton that year.
219.explanation: A woman of very small means measured her life not by what she owned but by how much good she could do with it.
219.tie_back: The kural says that for a kind-hearted person the only real poverty is being unable to do the good deeds that are his nature, and McCarty's one regret was that she did not have more to give.
219._accuracy_note: Her wish that she had more to give captures the kural's redefinition of poverty well, though she herself did not suffer a fall from wealth.

220.event_title: Oskar Schindler spends his fortune to protect his Jewish workers
220.event: Oskar Schindler, a German businessman and Nazi Party member who had grown rich in occupied Krakow, moved his armaments factory to Brunnlitz in 1944 and devoted himself until liberation in May 1945 to protecting its roughly 1,000 Jewish prisoners, paying for scarce food and medicine himself and deceiving the SS with false production figures. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum records that this required him to spend the fortune he had made in Krakow; he later claimed to have spent 2.64 million Reichsmarks. After the war he struggled financially and failed in business, and in 1993 Yad Vashem named him and his wife Emilie Righteous Among the Nations.
220.explanation: Schindler gave up a fortune and ended his life in financial hardship, but the more than 1,000 people he helped are why he is remembered.
220.tie_back: The kural says that if helping others brings ruin, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself, and Schindler exchanged his wealth for the survival of the people in his care.
220._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's ruin worth buying, though the kural speaks of ordinary beneficence and Schindler's earlier conduct was far from saintly.
